*In ancient Greece, for all her heroes, for Medea ... water meant death.*
— Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*

I poured a bowl of cereal, then tossed the empty box into the trash. Granddaddy retrieved it, shook the last crumbs into a bowl, and drowned the dust in milk. He stared down at the bowl, murmuring about how he'd survived the Depression. He told me of asking for hot water at colored diners, how he'd stir ketchup into a cup to make soup. This is how I first learned that I am wasteful.

•

I would stand in the bathroom with my mother, asking why the water in the bowl ran red. She told me she'd eaten beets. I suppose I was too young then to know the truth — that milk-flowers, when they bloom, spill petals of red.

•

In my Catholic school of fish, we passed a beautifully wrapped box from hand to hand, unwrapping it piece by piece. Afterward, it was explained to us — cleverly, we were told — that the box was a girl's virginity: the gift we give our husbands. And who wants a toy that has already been opened? Half the joy, after all, is in untying the string. This is how I learned that at my very core, I am ungrateful.

•

I met someone recently, in an Irish bar, who told me it's about knowing what I need. Later, he said: *what you need is a wife.*

---

# Lessons in Lack

I remember my grandfather's hands, weathered and sure, pulling a box of cereal from the trash can—not because it had spoiled, but because half of it remained, sacrificed to a spill or a stale taste or some other minor domestic sin. He held it up like evidence in a trial where I was already guilty. Then came the stories: the Depression, the bread lines, the way his own mother stretched a single egg across a family of six. I was maybe seven years old, and I learned that morning that wastefulness lived in me, inherited like eye color, something to be monitored and corrected. The cereal went back into the cabinet. I understood, without anyone saying it directly, that I took too much and gave back too little. That I was the kind of person who needed watching.

Some years later, in the fluorescent hush of a bathroom, my mother crouched beside me with a washcloth and a story about beets. Beets, she said, though we both knew the stain wasn't beets, though beets don't grow inside a body and seep out unannounced. I was young enough to believe her, or young enough to need to. What I understood, beneath the lie, was that whatever was happening to me was something to be renamed, softened, spoken around rather than spoken to. My body had begun doing something true, and the truth required a euphemism to be bearable. I learned that my body's realities were not to be discussed plainly, even by the person who knew me best. Especially not by her.

Then, in a classroom that smelled like chalk and candle wax, a teacher held up a box wrapped in shining paper and asked us to imagine unwrapping it, then wrapping it again, unwrapping it, wrapping it—until the paper tore, until the ribbon lost its curl, until the box itself, however whole on the inside, looked used. This, she explained, was what happened to a girl who did not wait. I was maybe twelve, sitting in a plastic chair, understanding for the first time that my body was not fully mine—it was a gift, held in trust, meant for a man I had not yet met, and that any unwrapping I did on my own was theft. Theft from him. Theft from God. I learned to feel already ungrateful for a gift I hadn't even given away yet, as if the wanting itself were a kind of spending.

Looking back, I see the pattern stitched through all of it: scarcity, purity, gratitude—three different words pointing at the same lesson. That my needs, my body, my truths were resources to be rationed, guarded, and eventually surrendered to someone else's accounting. The cereal, the blood, the box—each one taught me that I was a container for something precious that I could not be trusted to manage myself. Someone else had to hold the ledger. Someone else had to decide when I'd taken enough, given enough, kept myself pure enough.

Years later, in a bar dim with string lights and spilled beer, I sat across from a man who asked what I wanted—from a partner, from a life. I started to answer, something halting about companionship, about being known. He waved a hand before I finished. "So, a wife," he said, like he was closing a math problem, like every want I might name could be reduced to a single, tidy noun. I felt the old shape settle over me again: not a person with needs, but a role waiting to be filled, a box someone else got to open. I laughed, because it was easier than saying that I was tired—tired of being defined by what I could give rather than what I contained, tired of being told, in a hundred different ways, since I was seven years old, that I was too much and not enough at the very same time.

# What They Taught Us to Want

**I.**
My grandmother saved bacon grease in coffee cans,
counted eggs like rosary beads, whispered
*waste not* until the words wore grooves
into her tongue. She remembers standing
in bread lines longer than her own shadow,
learning that hunger was a private shame,
something to hide behind a straight back
and a mended dress. *We didn't complain,*
she says, as if complaint were another luxury
rationed out, another thing women
weren't allowed to want.

**II.**
My father tells it differently—
the diner on Route 9, the counter
where he wasn't allowed to sit,
where his hunger had to wait
outside in the car, in the heat,
while white families ate inside,
forks clinking like small bells
of belonging he could hear
but never touch. He learned early
that his need was a public offense,
that wanting to eat where others ate
was itself a kind of trespass.

**III.**
My mother, when I bled for the first time,
handed me a box without meeting my eyes,
said *you'll need these now* and nothing more—
no biology, no blood as anything
but evidence to be hidden, folded small,
disposed of quickly, discussed never.
I learned my body was a problem
to be managed, a leak to be stopped,
a fact to be ashamed of
even as it happened *to* me,
*inside* me, without my asking.

**IV.**
In seventh grade, Mrs. Halloway held up
a stick of gum, unwrapped it slowly
before the whole class, let it sit
exposed on her desk, gathering dust,
gathering our stares. *Would you want this now?*
she asked, and we all knew the answer
she wanted—no one wants
what's already been touched,
already been opened. She wrapped
our worth in cellophane that day,
told us our value lived
in staying sealed.

**V.**
So when the man at the party asked
what I wanted from my life,
and I began to speak of the novel
half-finished in my drawer,
the fellowship I'd applied for,
the mountain I meant to climb
before I turned thirty—

he smiled the smile of someone
who already knows the ending,
patted my hand, said *sure, sure,
but don't you just want
someone to take care of you?
A husband? Kids? Isn't that
what a woman really wants?*

And I felt it then—
all of it at once—
the bacon grease and the diner counter,
the box handed over without words,
the gum growing stale on the desk,
every lesson in scarcity
and shame and staying sealed
collapsing into his question,
as if my whole life
were just a longer way
of saying *yes.*

---

*I did not say yes.
I am still learning
how to say
everything else.*

# Echoes of Medea: Myth and Memory in Jesmyn Ward's Fiction

In the ancient tragedies of Greece, few figures loom as large or as troubling as Medea—the sorceress who, betrayed by Jason, commits the unthinkable act of killing her own children. Euripides gave voice to a woman whose rage and grief exceeded the boundaries of what Greek society could comfortably contain. Medea has haunted Western literature for over two thousand years precisely because she refuses easy categorization: she is victim and perpetrator, mother and destroyer, a woman pushed to extremity by forces both personal and cosmic.

It is this ancient, unsettling figure that the acclaimed American author Jesmyn Ward summons in her 2011 novel *Salvage the Bones*. Set in rural Mississippi in the days surrounding Hurricane Katrina, the novel follows Esch, a pregnant fifteen-year-old girl, as she reads and rereads the myth of Medea throughout the narrative. This is no accidental literary flourish. Ward uses the Greek story as a mirror and a lens, allowing Esch—and readers—to process the impending storm, the fractures within her family, and her own uncertain passage into motherhood.

The choice is a striking one. Why would a novel steeped in the specific textures of Black Southern life, in the rhythms of a fictional town called Bois Sauvage, reach back to ancient Greece for its mythological scaffolding? Ward's answer seems to be that Medea's story is not bound by geography or era. The themes she embodies—female rage, the precariousness of motherhood, betrayal, survival against overwhelming odds—are human constants. By threading Medea through her narrative, Ward elevates Esch's personal crisis to something with the weight of epic, suggesting that the struggles of a poor Black teenager in Mississippi deserve the same literary gravity as those of a mythic queen.

There is also a quiet, powerful reclamation happening here. Classical literature has long been treated as the exclusive inheritance of a particular tradition, often divorced from the lives of those like Esch and her family. Ward's invocation of Medea insists otherwise: that these ancient stories belong to everyone, that they can be read, absorbed, and repurposed by anyone seeking to understand their own circumstances. Esch doesn't merely read about Medea—she recognizes herself in her, drawing strength and language from a woman who lived, if she lived at all, millennia ago and an ocean away.

Hurricane Katrina itself becomes a kind of modern Fury, an elemental force as devastating and amoral as the gods who orchestrate Medea's tragedy. Ward suggests that just as the Greeks understood catastrophe as woven into the fabric of existence—arbitrary, merciless, yet somehow meaningful—so too must Esch's family navigate their own encounter with disaster, both natural and human-made.

In weaving Greece and Mississippi, myth and memoir-like realism, Ward performs a kind of literary alchemy. She reminds us that stories persist because they capture something essential about the human condition—about mothers and children, about survival and sacrifice, about the terrible choices people make when cornered by circumstance. Medea's ancient scream of grief and fury finds an unexpected echo in the flooded, wind-torn landscape of contemporary Mississippi, proving that some stories, however old, never stop being urgent.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in sections (using • as dividers) that opens with a quoted epigraph from Jesmyn Ward's "Salvage the Bones," then explores memories of poverty, menstruation, and purity culture, ending with a stranger's comment in a bar.
counterfactuals.output:
*"I am a girl, and even here, even now, blood means I am becoming something the world will try to name before I do."*
—Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*



The trailer had one window
that opened, and my mother
propped it with a paint can
so summer could get in
sideways, gasping.

We ate government cheese
sliced thin as communion wafers,
called it a meal, called it
enough, the way you call
a slap a lesson
when you're small enough
to need the hand
that gives it.



I was eleven in a gas station bathroom,
fluorescent and humming,
when I found the rust-brown proof
of what nobody had warned me for.

I balled up my shorts
in a plastic bag from the counter,
walked home along the ditch
where cattails hid me
from the road,

thinking: *this is the body's poverty,
too—this bleeding you're not given
the words for, only the shame,
handed down like a coat
too big, that you grow into
whether you want to or not.*



At church camp they gave us
purity rings and paper hearts
to fold and unfold, fold and unfold,
until the crease wore white
and someone said *that's you now,
that's what he'll see.*

They never mentioned blood.
They never mentioned hunger.
They talked about vessels
like we were jars to be capped,
not girls who bled on schedule
with the moon and nobody's permission.

I wanted to ask what happens
to a vessel that's already cracked,
already patched with masking tape
and mercy,
already full of something
they didn't bless.



Some nights the body remembers
poverty in its blood sugar,
remembers shame in its shoulders,
curls in on itself like a fist
around a coin it's afraid
to spend.

I have unlearned so much
and still find scraps of it
in my mouth, in how I apologize
for taking up a chair,
for bleeding through a chair,
for being a girl
who came from nothing
and had to build
her worth
from the leftover parts.



Bar light, neon, a stranger
leaning close enough
that I could smell the bourbon
sweetening his words—

*You don't look like you had it hard,*
he said, like hardship
leaves a brand,
like poverty and blood and God's own hands
should've marked me plainer,

should've written it
somewhere he could read it
without having to ask,

without having to sit still
long enough
to hear the answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a personal, confessional poem about growing up poor and Black, weaving in a grandfather's Depression-era stories, a mother's evasions about menstruation, and a Catholic school lesson on virginity, ending with a man in a bar making a sexist remark.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Learned First

Grandpa told it slow, like scripture,
how the Depression ate men whole—
"We ate what we could catch,
wore what we could sew,
and still we sang on Sunday."
He'd laugh with no teeth in it,
say *we had nothing and made a nation of it*,
say *hunger teaches you your own name*.
I didn't understand yet
that his stories were maps
of how to survive being poor
and being Black in a country
that kept both like debts on a ledger,
compounding.

Momma never said the word.
Just handed me a pad wrapped in a paper bag
like contraband, said
*you'll need these now*,
eyes somewhere past my shoulder,
already leaving the room
before I could ask why
my body was suddenly a secret
kept from myself.
I learned shame
before I learned biology—
learned that some things
about being a girl
were spoken only in silence,
in bags, in looking away.

Sister Agnes at St. Bernadette's
drew a flower on the chalkboard,
petals folded shut,
said *purity is a pearl, girls—
lose it once and it's gone forever*,
as if we were only ever
the sum of what we hadn't done,
as if the boys in the next room
weren't drawing their own flowers,
weren't being told
anything about loss at all.

I carried all of it—
Grandpa's hunger,
Momma's paper bags,
Sister Agnes's folded flower—
into every room I'd ever walk into
being both poor and Black and girl,
learning early
that my body would always be
a story someone else was narrating.

Years later, in a bar that smelled of Sundays
gone wrong, a man leaned in,
said *you're pretty for a Black girl,
bet you're feisty in bed too*—
and I heard my grandfather's hunger,
my mother's silence,
Sister Agnes's chalk-white flower,
all of it rising up in me at once—
generations of women
taught to swallow,
to bag it up,
to fold quiet as petals—

and for the first time
in this whole inherited history
of going without,
I said *no*.
Just that.
Small as a struck match,
loud as everything
that came before it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a lyrical prose-poem with fragmented sections separated by bullet points, using an epigraph about water and death, and themes of scarcity, shame, and womanhood being commodified.
counterfactuals.output:
*"Water has no memory of the drowned—only the shape it made letting them under."*
— anonymous, riverside

—

There was a well in the village that ran dry every August, and the women learned to measure their thirst in teaspoons, in the length of time between one mouth and the next. I was born in the dry month. My mother says I came out already rationing my cries.

•

Someone taught me that a woman's body is a cistern. Something to be filled, sealed, guarded against evaporation. Don't let it spill, they said, meaning: don't let it be seen spilling. Meaning: what leaks from you is currency, and currency mishandled is shame.

•

The men at the market weighed rice in their palms before buying. I have been weighed like that. A stranger's hand testing the give of my wrist, deciding what I was worth in the currency of before-marriage, after-marriage, still-fertile, no-longer.

•

*Scarcity* is a word that tastes like metal, like a coin held too long under the tongue. We were told there wasn't enough — not enough grain, not enough rain, not enough good years — so we learned to want small, to keep our hungers folded neat as good linen. My grandmother folded her whole life that way. Creased at the knees from kneeling at other people's wells.

•

They say a woman drowning will pull down whoever tries to save her — that instinct overrides gratitude. I think about this when I think about my mother's hands, how they were always wet, always reaching, always slightly too tight around my wrist at the market, at the well, at the edge of any water deep enough to keep me.

•

Here is the arithmetic of my girlhood: one body, divided by expectation, multiplied by every eye that priced it. The remainder was called *shame* and I carried it like a jug on my head, unspilled, for years, until I understood the jug was empty. Had always been empty. That the weight I carried was only the fear of what people would say if I set it down.

•

The river takes the shape of whatever bed it's given. I have been that obedient. I have been that clear, that quiet, that made-to-be-looked-through.

•

But water also erodes. Given enough time, it becomes the thing that carves the canyon, not the thing poured into the cup.

•

My mother, at the end, asked only for water. Not grain, not rain, not the years back. Just water, cool, in a cup she held herself, no one measuring how much passed her lips. I think this is the only inheritance that mattered — the moment right before the dying, when finally, *finally*, no one was pricing her thirst.

•

I pour my own water now. I do not ration my mouth. When they ask what I am worth I tell them: ask the river what it's worth. Ask it while it's still moving. Ask it before they've dammed it and named the reservoir after some dead man's charity.

•

Ask me now, while I'm still moving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that begins with a literary quote about Medea and water, then moves through childhood vignettes—wasting food, a mother's lie about blood, a school metaphor comparing virginity to a wrapped gift—culminating in a man's remark about wanting a wife.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Water Remembers**

*"I have suffered what is not to be told; I fell into the water and did not drown, though the sea kept asking."*
—after Euripides, *Medea*

I.
At six I left rice curling on my plate,
white grains going cold as a held breath.
My grandmother said: *somewhere a field is crying
for what your mouth refuses.*
I thought of a field with a face,
water standing in its rows like grief
that has nowhere else to go.
I finished every grain after that,
afraid of drowning something
I couldn't see.

II.
When the blood came, my mother said
*it's from a scratch, nothing, go wash it*—
and I believed her the way children believe
the sky is solid enough to hold a bird.
Later I understood: she wasn't lying
about the blood, only about the shame
folded so small inside it,
a coin sewn into a hem,
something she meant to spend
on silence.

III.
In school they held a wrapped chocolate,
passed it hand to hand down every row—
*look, it's a little dirty now, a little less shiny.
Who would want it?*
I looked at my own hands after,
at the foil-bright girl I'd been told I was,
and understood desire as a kind of hoarding,
love as a thing that only wants
what no one else has touched.
I did not ask what happens
to the chocolate. I only learned
to keep myself folded, uneaten,
a gift no one gets to open twice.

IV.
A man once told me, over coffee going cold
the way rice goes cold, the way blood goes cold
on a pad hidden at the bottom of a bag—
*I just want a wife. Someone clean. Someone
who hasn't been around.*
And I thought of Medea in the sea-foam,
not drowning, only asked and asked
by the water what she'd give up
to be wanted—
and how she gave up everything,
and the water still did not stop asking.

I said nothing.
I only thought of the field, crying
for what a mouth refuses,
and wondered which of us
was the wasted thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# What They Taught Me to Save

**I.**

My mother cut coupons like scripture,
folded Sunday circulars into a fan
she'd wave over the kitchen table,
teaching me the gospel of *not yet, not yet, wait for it to go on sale.*

She wore the same coat for eleven winters.
Called it good stewardship.
Called it thrift. Called it love, maybe,
the way she stretched a chicken into three dinners,
the way she said *we don't waste what we're given.*

I didn't know yet she was also talking about me.

**II.**

In seventh grade, Mrs. Halloran taped a rose
to the whiteboard, passed it hand to hand
around the room of girls in polo shirts,
told us to admire its velvet, its unbruised red.

By the time it reached the back row
it was ruined — petals bent, edges browning
where thirty nervous palms had gripped too hard.

*This*, she said, holding up the wilted thing
like evidence, *is what happens
when you give yourself away too soon.*

No one asked what happens to a flower
that's never touched at all.
No one asked why the boys
got to keep their hands in their pockets
and call it self-control.

**III.**

At home, we didn't throw out the ends of soap.
We pressed them together into new bars,
misshapen, striped like something scarred
but still good for washing.

I think about that soap sometimes
when I think about my body —
how I was told it was a whole bar once,
untouched, valuable only in its unbrokenness,

when really I was always something
being pieced together,
made from what came before,
useful in its patchwork,
clean in its own strange way.

**IV.**

My mother never said *virgin.*
She said *careful.*
She said *a boy only wants one thing*
the way she said *store brand's just as good* —
a lesson in economy, in guarding what's yours,
in knowing the going rate of things.

I didn't understand until much later
that she was teaching me to price myself,
to imagine my body a currency
that only lost value with use,

that no one ever taught her
a different math —
that a woman might be worth more
for what she's lived through,
not less.

**V.**

Here is what I know now:

The rose was always going to wilt.
That's what roses do.

The soap was never ruined,
just reshaped by use,
which is another word for *lived.*

And my mother, folding her coupons,
wearing her patient coat,
was trying to save me
from a world that taught her
scarcity was safety,
that closed hands were holy.

I want to tell her:
I opened my hands anyway.
I spent myself on people who mattered
and some who didn't
and I am still here,

not spent,
not ruined,
not a rose going brown at the edges —

just a woman
who stopped believing
her worth was something
that could run out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
